title: MoE expert prefetching and switch-cost field notes (Llama/Mistral/Qwen long-context)
body:
Purpose and quick summary:

This is a working note capturing empirical observations from a batch of microbenchmarks focused on MoE (sparse) routing costs under long-context workloads (8k–64k). Goal: identify where end-to-end token decode latency is dominated by expert switching and data movement, and sketch low-effort mitigations that the runtime team can implement quickly.

TL;DR findings (short):
- Expert switch latency (select + load expert weights / activations) is a non-trivial fraction of per-token tail for long-context decodes: measured ~8–35% extra ms/token depending on model and routing sparsity.
- Prefetching expert KV/activation pages into GPU memory ahead of decode reduces stall time but increases steady-state memory pressure; best results when combined with a small LRU "expert working set" (4–8 experts pinned).
- Sticky routing heuristics (prefer previously-used experts within a session) reduced switch counts by ~18% in chat-like traces and cut tail latency more than mean latency.
- Qwen-style wider attention + larger head counts amplifies cost of expert switching due to more frequent cache thrash; Mistral was more forgiving because of smaller per-expert weight footprint.

Experiment environment (short):
- HW: 8x A100-SXM-80GB (NVLink), single-GPU microbench results isolated on one A100-SXM-80 for per-GPU numbers. Also used a 4xH100 cluster for a few multi-GPU distributed runs.
- Runtime: current main branch + perf hooks (PR 814 linked above) that log: routing-selection time, expert-weight-transfer time, expert-activation-load time, and stall time waiting for expert data.
- Models: Llama-2-13B MoE variant (2\u003e experts per router), Mistral-MoE-7B-ish (internal staging), Qwen-MoE-14B config (prototype weights).
- Context traces: two synthetic traces + one production chat trace (anonymized):
  - synth-bursty: repeated short queries where routing changes per query (high expert churn)
  - synth-sticky: requests with high locality (same tokens -> same experts)
  - prod-chat-sampled: 1200 sessions, avg 3.8 turns/session, mean turn length 420 tokens, some long tails to 4k tokens.

Key metrics recorded (per-token windows):
- total_decode_ms_per_token (avg / p95 / p99)
- routing_decision_ms (softmax + top-k select + any routing heuristics)
- expert_transfer_ms (time to move expert weights/kv/activations onto GPU local memory)
- stall_wait_ms (waiting for data ready)
- extra_mem_usage_mb (due to pinned experts / prefetch buffers)

Representative microbenchmark results (single-GPU, decode step steady-state, numbers = mean ms/token):
- Llama-2-MoE-13B, bursty: baseline (no prefetch): total 7.2 ms/token, stall_wait 1.6 ms/token (22%); with prefetch+working-set(6 experts) total 6.0 ms/token, stall_wait 0.4 ms/token (6.6%), extra_mem +6.9GB. p95 reduction ~28%
- Mistral-MoE-7B, bursty: baseline total 5.4 ms/token, stall_wait 0.9 ms/token (17%); prefetch total 4.9 ms/token, stall_wait 0.3 ms/token; extra_mem +3.1GB
- Qwen-MoE-14B, bursty: baseline total 9.8 ms/token, stall_wait 2.9 ms/token (30%); prefetch total 8.3 ms/token, stall_wait 0.9 ms/token; extra_mem +9.7GB

Observations and interpretation:
1) Two dominant contributors to switch cost:
   - control-plane decision (routing select compute): cheap in absolute but spikes when software routing is done on CPU or through an inefficient kernel. For our runtime, routing_decision_ms is ~0.2–0.6ms and is not the main target.
   - data movement (weights/kv/activations move from slower tiers / other GPUs / host memory into local GPU memory): this is the big one. When an expert not present locally is selected, we pay a transfer cost + potential cache eviction churn.

2) Prefetching strategy matters:
   - naive prefetch (fetch experts for predicted next-token selections) can reduce stalls but must be coupled with a working set policy (max pinned experts) to avoid OOM on 80GB-class cards.
   - best performer: a randomized weighted prefetch + LRU eviction. Weight: predicted selection probability from routing logits + recency score.
   - prefetch horizon of 1 token works well for greedy decode; with sampling / top-k sampling it needs horizon 2–5 to capture stochasticity, which increases memory cost.

3) Sticky-routing heuristics give good bang for little complexity:
   - heuristic: if chosen expert at t-1 had selection probability within top-3 for t, prefer it unless energy diff > threshold. This reduces inter-token expert churn for dialog-like inputs.
   - in prod-chat-sampled trace, sticky reduced number of new expert loads by 18% and reduced p95 decode tail by ~16%.

4) Interaction with KV cache and long-context:
   - long KV cache size (64k) increases memory pressure and exacerbates expert eviction thrash. When an expert is evicted, its cached activations must be reconstructed or swapped back in, which costs both time and memory.
   - a prioritized eviction policy that considers KV cache hotness (how recently tokens touching that expert were used) helps: we saw 10–14% fewer re-loads vs naive LRU.

5) Model-specific notes:
   - Llama variants: large expert weight sizes per expert -> prefetch needs are heavier; on-card memory consumption is the limiting factor.
   - Mistral: lighter expert kernels allow keeping a slightly larger working set, which reduces stalls with less memory hit.
   - Qwen: broader attention and larger intermediate size make expert activations bigger; transfer costs scale with activation size more than weight size here.

Micro-profiling snippets (examples) — these are lines from the PR814 perf log for a single decode session:
  [step 178] routing_decision_ms=0.28 expert_idx=[3,7] expert_transfer_ms=1.22 expert_activation_load_ms=0.60 stall_wait_ms=1.86 total_ms=8.3
  [step 179] routing_decision_ms=0.21 expert_idx=[3,7] expert_transfer_ms=0.00 expert_activation_load_ms=0.05 stall_wait_ms=0.03 total_ms=5.9
  [step 401] routing_decision_ms=0.33 expert_idx=[12] expert_transfer_ms=2.05 expert_activation_load_ms=0.88 stall_wait_ms=2.9 total_ms=11.1

Quick wins (actionable, low-effort):
- Implement async expert prefetch API in runtime: allow selection kernel to enqueue DMA for predicted experts while current token is being processed. This is ~2–3 days dev + 1 day of integration tests.
- Add "expert working set" config per deployment (default 6 for 80GB, 10 for 160GB), expose via model manifest.
- Implement sticky-routing flag that can be enabled for workload classes (chat, instruction-following) in rollout. Cheap to add (1–2 engineer-days) and measurable benefit.
- Instrumentation: add counters for "expert-loads-per-session", "expert-reload-bytes", and histogram of consecutive-same-expert run lengths. These are necessary to qualify effectiveness of prefetch heuristics.

Medium/longer term opportunities:
- Kernel-level expert weight residency management: maintain small on-GPU compressed forms of all experts (quantized / fused) and expand to full precision on demand. This would reduce transfer size. Investigate quantization + fused decompress kernel.
- Cross-GPU expert locality heuristics leveraging NVLink: prefer selecting experts that are local or reachable via NVLink with lower latency for a given request, unless model-quality cost is high. Needs scheduler + routing-policy coordination.
- Hybrid schedule: batch decode across sessions to amortize expert loads when possible. Batching helps if many sessions select same experts around the same time — but increases latency for individual requests. Worth exploring in Dedicated clusters with predictable SLAs.

Open questions / unknowns (we should test):
- How does higher sampling temperature affect prefetch horizon tradeoffs across Llama vs Qwen? We saw sampling increases expert unpredictability but need a wider sample set.
- Multi-GPU distributed routing: quantify NVLink vs PCIe staging costs with more model configs (H100 runs were limited).
- Interaction with quantized expert storage: what is the runtime CPU/GPU overhead to dequantize on load? Does it cancel out transfer savings?

Rough implementation plan / milestones (next 6 weeks):
- Week 1–2: land perf counters + lightweight sticky-routing flag (PR 814 continues).
- Week 3: async prefetch API + simple prefetcher (prefetch horizon 1, working set cap). Run nightly perf-bench across traces.
- Week 4–5: evaluate prefetch heuristics (probability-weighted, recency-augmented). Tune defaults per model family.
- Week 6: decision point: ship in beta for Dedicated clusters / feature flag behind runtime config.

Notes to self / random observations:
- When profiling, make sure GPU->CPU memcpy logging is on; some of the biggest stalls were mislabeled until we turned on the memcpy trace.
- For Mistral-MoE staging, weight sharding across experts is more favorable — we should check our model-import path to see if it preserves shard locality.
- There are a few Slack threads with benchmarks vs competitor runtimes; capture them in confluence and compare once sticky + prefetch is live.

References / links in one place: PR 814 (perf hooks), internal confluence proposal (linked above), JIRA-ENG-3267 for the prefetch epic.

Attachments we should create next:
- short slide deck (2–3 slides) showing p95 improvement with prefetch+sticky for each model family (Llama, Mistral, Qwen) — useful for product sign-off.
- small benchmark harness (repo snippet) that can reproduce synth-bursty and synth-sticky traces with seeds and config.

End of note.

Unresolved: choose default working_set size per GPU memory class and whether to enable sticky-routing by default for hosted API (privacy / determinism implications).

-- Priya
